source_reviews.independent_solution: A connected circuit driven continually by an externally applied periodically varying emf or voltage has forced electrical oscillations. The steady response follows the driving frequency, not an obligatory natural-frequency match. In a passive lossy circuit, periodic stored energy implies external net work per cycle replaces dissipation. Initial capacitor charge alone supplies only a free decaying transient, and constant DC does not maintain periodic forcing.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For a fixed positive pure resistance R, u(t)=R i(t). A sinusoid i=I_m sin(omega t+phi) produces u=R I_m sin(omega t+phi), so voltage and current share frequency, phase, zeros and corresponding extrema. Amplitudes satisfy U_m=R I_m, and RMS values over the same interval satisfy U=RI.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For a sinusoid averaged over a complete cycle, U^2=U_m^2/2. source_reviews.independent_solution: For an interval of duration Delta t, I=sqrt((1/Delta t) integral i(t)^2 dt) and U=sqrt((1/Delta t) integral u(t)^2 dt), taking nonnegative roots. The squares are inside the time average. Complete periods give conventional periodic RMS. Equivalent DC magnitudes produce the same average heating on the same fixed resistance, not equal instantaneous values. Signed mean and peak are not general RMS definitions, and peak/sqrt(2) requires the sinusoidal whole-period case.

Integrating the energy balance over one steady period gives Delta E_stored=0 and W_source=integral R i(t)^2 dt. option_checks.evidence: Continually applied periodic emf is an external forcing, rather than an initial condition; this matches the author's periodic-drive derivation.

With only the initial capacitor charge and no subsequent source, resistive heat reduces stored energy each cycle. Treating this finite charge as continuing external drive produces precisely the stated free-versus-forced misconception.

A constant-magnitude, constant-direction emf has no periodic forcing. Identifying any continuously connected source as an oscillatory source ignores time dependence and yields this false option; startup transients are not the required steady state.
At steady-period endpoints the stored energy repeats, so net source work equals resistive heat per cycle. The statement concerns integrated energy, not identical instantaneous source and loss powers.

A quarter-cycle shift would break simultaneous zeros, and a negative multiplier would reverse signs. Only C is true, matching the author after the independent solution was saved.

mathematics.independent_solution: Over period T, I=sqrt((1/T) integral i^2 dt) and U=sqrt((1/T) integral u^2 dt), with nonnegative roots. For i=sin(omega t), signed mean is 0 but RMS is 1/sqrt(2); for u=sin(omega t), max|u|=1 but RMS is 1/sqrt(2). Thus A,C are the complete true set. Special waveforms can have peak=RMS, but that coincidence does not make the peak a general definition. The author agrees with these independent results.

option_checks.evidence: A squares instantaneous current first, averages i^2 in time and finally takes the nonnegative root: sqrt(overline(i^2)), not sqrt(overline(i)^2).

C applies the same operation order to voltage: u^2 stays inside the complete-cycle time average and its nonnegative square root lies outside.

For a nonzero sinusoid the largest absolute voltage is U_m while RMS is U_m/sqrt(2). Replacing the interval mean-square measure by the maximum gives the author's peak-confusion procedure and a false general definition.
